sections.heading: Dialogue III, Knot x, part 1 (printed pp. 343–353)
rows: [Margin, p. 343: Nodus X. Fundamentum fati Stoicorum.]
[Margin, p. 343: Knot X. The foundation of the fate [fati] of the Stoics.]

Asphal. Ego vero reclamo huic iniquae duorum consensioni. Et quoniam tu non vis, Ereuni, utrique vestrum me oppono. Et quoniam alter Deum conditorem, alter gubernatorem asseruit, utrumque una sive collectione sive sententia convello.

Asphal. But I cry out against [reclamo] this unjust agreement [consensioni] of the two. And since you are not willing, Ereunius, I oppose myself to each of you. And since the one asserted God [to be] founder [conditorem], the other governor [gubernatorem], I tear up [convello] both with one, whether collection [collectione] or sentence [sententia].

Fuit autem antiquorum Stoicorum virorum, nosti, quanta doctrina; quamvis (ut fateor) non satis mihi videntur constanter suis adhaesisse principiis. Eorum nihilosecius nomine dicam: utrique scribo, tibi inprimis, Andabata. Age itaque non habes certum, contradictorias ita se habere ut una sit vera, & altera falsa?

Now there was, of the ancient Stoic men, you know how great a learning [doctrina]; although (as I confess) they do not seem to me to have adhered constantly enough to their own principles. In their name nonetheless I shall speak: I write [scribo] to each, to you in the first place, Andabata. Come then, do you not hold [it] certain that contradictories [contradictorias] are so disposed [ita se habere] that one is true and the other false?
Andab. Habeo.
Andab. I hold [it].
Asphal. Et hoc ex necessitate? adeo ut contrarium sit impossibile.
Asphal. And this from necessity? so much that the contrary is impossible.

Andab. Et quidem quam maxime ut nihil magis impossibile esse possit. Impossibilitas siquidem omnis ex implicatione contradictionis nascitur: quare maxima impossibilitas, & formalissima est contradictionem existere, seu contradictorias esse simul veras.

Andab. And indeed as much as possible, so that nothing can be more impossible. Since every impossibility is born from the implication [implicatione] of contradiction: wherefore the greatest impossibility, and the most formal [formalissima], is [for] a contradiction to exist, or [for] contradictories to be true at the same time.
Asphal. Et hoc extendit se ad omnes contradictorias, etiam de futuro pronunciatas, & de illo etiam futuro quod contingens vocant, quod si causas solas respiceremus, esse posset vel non esse.

Asphal. And this extends itself to all contradictories, even [those] pronounced about the future, and even about that future which they call contingent [contingens], which, if we looked to the causes alone, could be or not be.

Andab. Etiam hoc fateor: neque in his maiorem reperio dubitandi rationem quam in aliis, quandoquidem contradictio clare in iis cernitur, & tam clare quam in aliis quibusvis: contradictionem autem, ubicumque sit, sortiri suum effectum, id est, impossibilitatem efficere vel evidens est, vel ego scientiis renuncio.

Andab. This too I confess: nor do I find in these a greater reason [rationem] for doubting than in others, since the contradiction is clearly discerned in them, and as clearly as in any others whatever: and that a contradiction, wherever it be, obtains [sortiri] its effect, that is, effects impossibility, either is evident, or I renounce the sciences [scientiis].
Asphal. Non itaque aliunde quaerendum est cur una sit falsa altera vera, quam quia contradictoriae sunt.
Asphal. Not from elsewhere, then, is it to be sought why one is false, the other true, than because they are contradictories.
Andab. Sic existima.
Andab. So judge [existima].

Asphal. In communi loqueris an vero in particulari: hoc est dicisne in communi dumtaxat unam habere veritatem, & aliam habere falsitatem, ex vi contradictionis, an etiam in particulari hanc esse veram, illam esse falsam ex vi eiusdem contradictionis?

Asphal. Do you speak in common [in communi] or rather in particular [in particulari]: that is, do you say only in common that one has truth and the other has falsity, from the force [ex vi] of the contradiction, or also in particular that this [one] is true, that [one] is false, from the force of the same contradiction?

Andab. Nescio ego utrum haec aut illa sit vera vel falsa; sed unam earum esse veram scio, & alteram falsam, utra sit nescio, neque possum dicere hanc esse determinate veram; sed possum dicere, si non sit determinate vera, esse determinate falsam. Et hoc ex vi contradictionis, ut assumpsisti.

Andab. I do not know whether this or that is true or false; but that one of them is true I know, and the other false; which [of the two] it is I do not know, nor can I say that this [one] is determinately [determinate] true; but I can say, if it is not determinately true, that it is determinately false. And this from the force of the contradiction, as you assumed.
Asphal. Ergo indeterminatio quam ponis, tantummodo respectu nostri est, quia ignorantes sumus, non autem respectu rei quae omnimodam determinationem habet.

Asphal. Therefore the indetermination [indeterminatio] which you posit is only in respect of us, because we are ignorant, but not in respect of the thing, which has an every-way [omnimodam] determination.
Andab. Hoc est quod dico.
Andab. This is what I say.

Asphal. Ergo sic se habent hae propositiones, sicut propositiones de praesenti vel praeterito, de quibus prorsus ignari sumus, v. g. dicatur, Corvus cras transvolabit Gangem vel Nigrum: & Corvus dum loquor, transvolat Gangem, seu heri transvolavit, eadem prorsus est ratio harum trium propositionum, quoad determinationem veritatis, & quoad indeterminationem quoad nos: & quoad causam determinationis, quoad se. Quid haeres?

Asphal. Therefore these propositions are so disposed [sic se habent] as propositions about the present or past, about which we are entirely ignorant; e.g. let it be said, ‘A raven tomorrow will fly across the Ganges or the Niger [Nigrum]’: and ‘A raven, while I speak, flies across the Ganges’, or ‘yesterday flew across’: entirely the same is the account [ratio] of these three propositions, as to the determination of truth, and as to the indetermination as to us: and as to the cause of the determination, as to itself [quoad se]. Why do you stick [haeres]?
Andab. Frustra haerebam: prorsus enim concedendum est, & asserendum contradictionis vim quoad ipsam rem, aequaliter se habere ad omnes has propositiones.

Andab. In vain I was sticking: for it is entirely to be conceded, and to be asserted, that the force of the contradiction, as to the thing itself, stands equally [aequaliter se habere] to all these propositions.
Asphal. Etiamne ad earum obiecta? Rursus haeres.
Asphal. Even to their objects [obiecta]? Again you stick.

Andab. Nequaquam: iacta est alea, etiam ad earum obiecta, eandem vim habet. Evidens enim est veritatem propositionum vel falsitatem non esse aliud quam conformitatem vel deformitatem ad obiecta: Et rursus si in {?proportionibus} sit contradictio, eas non posse esse conformes obiectis, nisi sit etiam contradictio in obiectis; neque posse esse veram aliquam propositionem nisi obiectum sit, sicut ipsa dicit, neque falsam, nisi non sit, sicut ipsa enunciat.

Andab. By no means: the die is cast [iacta est alea]; even to their objects it has the same force. For it is evident that the truth or falsity of propositions is not other than conformity or deformity [deformitatem] to the objects: And again, if in the {?proportions} [proportionibus, for propositionibus] there be contradiction, they cannot be conformable to the objects unless there be also contradiction in the objects; nor can any proposition be true unless the object be as it itself says, nor false unless it be not as it itself enunciates [enunciat].
Asphal. Sicut ergo res existens necessario est dum est, quia est: sic res futura necessario est futura dum est futura, quia est futura.
Asphal. As therefore an existing thing necessarily is while it is, because it is: so a future thing necessarily is future while it is future, because it is future.
Andab. Audenter dico.
Andab. I say [so] boldly.

Asphal. Et ego non minori confidentia assero, si haec vera sunt, neque conditorem ullum esse mundi posse, neque gubernatorem: Sed quaecumque sunt esse quia sunt, & fato Stoico, hoc est contradictionis necessitate cuncta nasci & denasci, & rem universi geri.

Asphal. And I with no less confidence assert, if these [things] are true, that there can be neither any founder [conditorem] of the world nor governor: But that whatever things are, are because they are; and that by Stoic fate [fato], that is, by the necessity of contradiction, all things are born and un-born [denasci], and the affair of the universe [rem universi] is carried on [geri].
Andab. Magnifice, Asphali, modo gesta verbis non responsent.
Andab. Magnificently [said], Asphalius, only [modo] the deeds [gesta] do not answer [responsent] to the words.

[sic: Andab.] Tu vero, Andabata, ipse te iudicem praesta, sed aequum & ab ipso dictorum tuorum praeiudicio liberum. Nonne quae facta sunt, infecta facere, neque Deo permissum, & Philosophia & Logica & communis hominum sensus testatur.

[Asphal.; printed Andab.] But you, Andabata, show yourself [praesta] judge yourself, but [a judge] fair and free from the very prejudgement [praeiudicio] of your own sayings. Do not both Philosophy and Logic and the common sense of men testify that to make things which have been done [facta] undone [infecta] is not permitted even to God?
Andab. Novi, itaque ignarus iam dudum sum quo tendas, sed perge.
Andab. I know [it]; and so [itaque] I have long now been ignorant [ignarus] where you are heading, but proceed.
Asphal. Sed & quae sunt dum sunt, facta sunt pro eo tempore quo sunt. Nulla itaque potestas etiam est, ut quod est, non sit dum est.
Asphal. But also the things which are, while they are, are done [facta] for that time in which they are. There is therefore also no power [potestas] that what is, should not be while it is.
Andab. Clarissimum etiam hoc est.
Andab. This too is most clear.
Asphal. Quare & de futuris tantumdem dicendum est, dum futura sunt non posse fieri ne futura sint.
Asphal. Wherefore just as much is to be said of future things too: [that] while they are future, it cannot come about that they not be future.
Andab. Et hoc etiam accipe, nihil enim quicquam evidentius fingi potest.
Andab. And this too accept [as granted], for nothing whatever more evident can be fashioned [fingi].
Asphal. Et quae futura sunt semper fuerunt futura, quare nunquam non potuerunt fieri non futura.
Asphal. And the things which are future always were future; wherefore never could they not [nunquam non potuerunt] become not-future.
Andab. Etiam hoc accipe.
Andab. This too accept.
Asphal. Et hoc habent ex vi contradictionis, sicut quod est aut fuit esse vel fuisse: hoc enim iam ante concessisti; negare iam non est licitum.
Asphal. And this they have from the force of contradiction, as what is or was [has it] to be or to have been: for this you already conceded before; to deny [it] now is not permitted.
Andab. Nihil dubita, non sum negaturus.
Andab. Doubt nothing, I am not going to deny [it].

Asphal. Vide itaque num etiam hoc non clarum sit, habere non posse non esse pro eo tempore pro quo futura sunt. Et hoc non ab alio sed a contradictione inclusa in ipsamet obiecti essentia, quorum duorum hoc ultimum excludit causam extrinsecam essendi, prius vero gubernandi potestatem.

Asphal. See therefore whether this too is not clear: [that they] have [it] that they cannot not be for that time for which they are future. And this not from another but from the contradiction included in the very essence of the object; of which two [points] this last excludes an extrinsic cause of being, but the former [prius] the power of governing.

Quae enim gubernatio est, ubi aliter res fieri non possunt? vel quae causa illius quod ab intrinseca necessitate habet ut existat: dic enim qua alia necessitate Deus existit a se & causam habere non potest, sed formaliter est sua existentia?

For what government [gubernatio] is there where things cannot come about otherwise? or what cause of that which has from an intrinsic necessity that it exist: for tell [me], by what other necessity does God exist from himself [a se], and cannot have a cause, but is formally [formaliter] his own existence?

Andab. Nondum matura est victoria tua paeani. Manet enim te adhuc inexpectata fortassis solutio: Quae enim concessi, omnia non absolute dicta sunt, sed ex suppositione: quae autem ex suppositione dicuntur, nullam vim inferunt absolutis, sed necessitatem dumtaxat ex suppositione faciunt.

Andab. Your victory is not yet ripe for the paean [paeani]. For there still awaits you a perhaps unexpected solution: For the things which I conceded were all said not absolutely but from supposition [ex suppositione]: but things which are said from supposition bring no force [vim] upon absolute [things], but make only a necessity from supposition.

Asphal. Fateor inexpectatam. Per tot enim interrogationes elicere conabar & semper expectabam & obstructam iam illi viam credebam, cum ecce subito erumpit. Sed age quae est illa suppositio ex qua respondebas interrogatis?

Asphal. I confess [it] unexpected. For through so many questions I was trying to draw [it] out, and was always expecting [it], and believed the way already blocked to it, when lo, suddenly it breaks out. But come, what is that supposition from which you were answering the things asked?

Andab. Nempe haec, signatam propositionem esse veram & oppositam falsam. Etsi enim concedebam unam esse determinate veram & alteram falsam, tamen eam quae esset vera, signare me posse negabam. Ignarus enim integre sum utra sit. Ut itaque concludatur hanc esse veram, suppositione fit, non rerum natura.

Andab. Namely this: that the designated [signatam] proposition is true and the opposite false. For although I conceded that one is determinately true and the other false, yet I denied that I could designate [signare] that which was true. For I am wholly ignorant which [of the two] it is. So that it be concluded, then, that this [one] is true, comes about by supposition, not by the nature of things.

Asphal. Non itaque meministi me hoc suscepisse, hanc indeterminationem dumtaxat respectu tui & mei esse, in re vero abstrahendo a me & te, nullam esse indeterminationem, atque totam deinde argumentationem de existentia in natura harum propositionum extitisse, unde nullus iam locus recurrendi ad suppositionem.

Asphal. Do you not, then, remember that I undertook [suscepisse] this: that this indetermination was only in respect of you and me, but in the thing, abstracting from me and you, there was no indetermination; and that the whole argumentation thereafter stood [extitisse] on the existence in nature of these propositions; whence [there is] now no place for recurring to supposition.

Andab. Non ipse tu modo supponis propositiones existere, & nisi hoc supponatur, quis disputationi locus, scimus enim propositiones non existere, vel certe non scimus existere. Manifestum itaque est ex necessitate recurrendum esse ad suppositiones.

Andab. Do you not yourself just now [modo] suppose that the propositions exist? and unless this be supposed, what place for disputation? for we know that the propositions do not exist, or certainly we do not know [them] to exist. It is manifest, therefore, that one must of necessity recur to suppositions.

Asphal. Ad hanc quidem suppositionem non diffiteor esse repedandum. Sed reliqua suppositio ex hac naturaliter sequitur: posito enim esse propositiones, alteram in ipsa re necessum est esse signate veram, reliquam signate falsam quantumvis nos eas designare non valeamus: Constas in hoc?

Asphal. To this supposition indeed I do not deny that one must go back [repedandum]. But the remaining supposition follows naturally from this: for, it being posited that there are propositions, it is necessary [necessum est] that one in the thing itself be designatedly [signate] true, the other designatedly false, however much we are not able to designate them: Do you stand firm [constas] in this?
Andab. Quid prodest, dum ulterior est suppositio in qua hoc fundatur?
Andab. What does it profit, while there is a further [ulterior] supposition on which this is founded?
Asphal. Age igitur quoniam in hac te Acropoli tutari certum est, hoc responde, sive sit aliqua propositio, sive non sit, non eodem modo sese habet obiectum?

Asphal. Come then, since it is settled [certum est] [for you] to defend yourself in this Acropolis, answer this: whether there be any proposition or there be not, is not the object disposed [sese habet] in the same way?
Andab. Habet utique.
Andab. It is so disposed [habet], certainly [utique].
Asphal. Ergo eadem est necessitas obiectorum (de qua est quaestio) sive supponamus aliquam propositionem esse, sive non esse.
Asphal. Therefore the necessity of the objects (about which is the question) is the same whether we suppose some proposition to be, or not to be.
Andab. Est ut dicis.
Andab. It is as you say.
Asphal. Quid ergo iam te moratur ne cedas?
Asphal. What then now delays you from yielding [ne cedas]?
Andab. Rursus suppositio, certe enim supponere debes obiectum esse futurum, & tantumdem valebat, etiam propositionem esse supponere.
Andab. Again supposition: for certainly you must suppose the object to be future, and [it] was worth just as much [tantumdem valebat] also to suppose the proposition to be.
Asphal. Ergo nisi ego supponam obiectum esse futurum, non erit futurum?
Asphal. Therefore unless I suppose the object to be future, it will not be future?

Andab. Immo erit. Sed non erit ex suppositione necessarium, nisi fiat suppositio: sicut vides, dum de praesenti loqueris, ipsum te addere dum praesens est. Nisi enim haec reduplicatio fieret, nulla necessitas foret.

Andab. Rather [immo], it will be. But it will not be necessary from supposition unless the supposition be made: as you see, while you speak about the present, [that] you yourself add ‘while it is present’. For unless this reduplication [reduplicatio] were made, there would be no necessity.

Asphal. Sed haec necessitas non est suppositionis: suppositio enim effectus quidam mentis est & in mente; haec autem verba non explicant quomodo in mente sese habeant res, sed quomodo in se: neque reduplicatio est τὸ dum, sed temporis designatio, quare neque futuri dum futurum est notatio, reduplicatio est, sed expressio conditionis rei.

Asphal. But this necessity is not of supposition: for a supposition is a certain effect of the mind and [is] in the mind; but these words do not unfold how things are disposed in the mind, but how [they are] in themselves: nor is the ‘while’ [τὸ dum] a reduplication, but a designation of time; wherefore neither is the notation [notatio] ‘of the future while it is future’ a reduplication, but an expression of the condition of the thing.
Andab. Audio, sed necdum evicisti. Ipsa enim futuritio ex suppositione est saltem causae ex ipsa natura sua, unde non excludit causam.

Andab. I hear, but you have not yet won the case [evicisti]. For futurition [futuritio] itself from supposition is at least of a cause [causae], from its very nature; whence it does not exclude a cause.

Asphal. Hoc vis dicere, quod sicut esse in praesenti facit essendi necessitatem ex vi contradictionis, & tamen habet causam; sic etiam futurum esse habet causam quantumvis ex contradictione faciat rem necessario fore.

Asphal. This you mean to say: that as to-be in the present makes a necessity of being from the force of contradiction, and yet has a cause; so also to-be-future [futurum esse] has a cause, however much from contradiction it makes the thing necessarily be-going-to-be [fore].

Verum hoc considerare oportet causam essendi in praesenti, actu esse: unde habet, ut vim contradictioni dare possit, causam autem futuri tantum in potentia esse, unde contradictioni nullum fundamentum suppeditare potest. Iam enim superius consensum est, non existens non habere vim per quam aliud esse possit.

But this one must consider: that the cause of being in the present is in act [actu]: whence it has [it] that it can give force to the contradiction; but the cause of the future is only in potency [in potentia]; whence it can supply no foundation to the contradiction. For already above it was agreed that the non-existent does not have a force through which another can be.

Andab. Ne tibi sic os sublini permittas, Asphali: habet enim futuritio suam quoque actu causam. Postquam enim Deum diximus singulos effectus & praenovisse & singulas eis circumstantias praestituisse; certe causam actu existere negare nullo modo potes.

Andab. Do not permit your mouth to be so smeared [os sublini, i.e. yourself to be so fooled], Asphalius: for futurition also has its cause in act. For after we said that God both foreknew [praenovisse] the single effects and pre-established [praestituisse] the single circumstances for them; certainly you can in no way deny the cause to exist in act.

Asphal. Nihilo secius, Andabata, tantumdem enim est causam non esse & non operari, nihil dum vero operatur in effectus futuros Deus. Cum enim non operetur in eos nisi per causas medias quae necdum positae erunt, si de plerisque effectis loquamur, nihil prodest tibi quod Deus ipse existat, qui olim haec effecta parturiat.

Asphal. None the less, Andabata; for it is just as much [tantumdem] for a cause not to be and not to operate; but God as yet [dum] operates nothing on future effects. For since he does not operate on them except through middle [medias] causes which will not yet have been posited [necdum positae erunt], if we speak of most effects, it profits you nothing that God himself exists, who will one day [olim] bring forth [parturiat] these effects.

Andab. Verum enimvero hac ipsa hora positae sunt causae, ex quibus necessario ii effectus orituri sunt qui horum de quibus loquimur, causae sint: & quoniam totum iter necessitatibus Adamantinis stratum est, iam futuritio in his ipsis causis est.

Andab. But truly, in this very hour causes have been posited from which necessarily those effects are going to arise which are the causes of these of which we speak: and since the whole road has been paved with Adamantine [Adamantinis] necessities, futurition is already in these very causes.

Asphal. Non itaque futuritionem vocas existentiam effectus in se pro tempore assignato, sed existentiam quam modo in causis habeant: [Margin, p. 352: Futuritionem rerum ex Dei essentia oriri.] In hac autem si colloces rationem futuritionis, contradictionis evacuas necessitatem quae inter effectum & non effectum pro illa hora reperitur; non autem inter effectum & non effectum, prout sunt in causa a qua per alias contingentes, effectus exiturus est in lucem, deseris itaque quaestionem si eam ab effectis ad causas removes.

Asphal. You do not, then, call futurition the existence of the effect in itself for the assigned time, but the existence which they now have in the causes: [Margin, p. 352: That the futurition of things arises from the essence of God.] But if you place the notion [rationem] of futurition in this, you empty [evacuas] the necessity of contradiction which is found between the effect and the non-effect for that hour; but not between the effect and the non-effect as they are in the cause from which, through other contingent [causes], the effect is going to go out into the light; you desert, therefore, the question if you remove it from the effects to the causes.

Andab. Non moveo quaestionem; sed sicut tu non diffiteris, quod praesens est ex necessitate contradictionis existere, & tamen hanc necessitatem a causa habere; sic ego ostendo futurum quamvis ex necessitate contradictionis sit futurum, causam tamen contradictionis & necessitatis habere.

Andab. I do not move the question; but as you do not deny that what is present exists from the necessity of contradiction, and yet has this necessity from a cause; so I show that the future, although it be future from the necessity of contradiction, yet has a cause of the contradiction and of the necessity.

Asphal. Et non advertis praesentis causam operatam esse, & quoniam operata est, ipsi contradictioni vim dedisse: in futuris autem nondum operatam esse causam, & proinde neque contradictionem a causa vim ullam habere posse. Quare si contradictio ullam vim habet, ex sese & non ex causa habere.

Asphal. And do you not notice that the cause of the present has operated, and since it has operated, has given force to the contradiction itself: but in future things the cause has not yet operated, and accordingly neither can the contradiction have any force from the cause? Wherefore, if the contradiction has any force, [it] has [it] from itself and not from the cause.

Andab. Immo tu non advertis de cognitione nobis quaestionem esse; cognitioni vero satis esse ut obiectum quoad speciem sit determinatum, & non requiri ut actu existentiam habeat; ex eo autem quod ipsa prima causarum dispositio facta est, determinatam exinde esse obiecti speciem; puta quaenam duarum obiecti partium sit futura, & si neutri communicata sit existentia:

Andab. Rather [immo] you do not notice that the question for us is about cognition [cognitione]; but that for cognition it is enough that the object be determined as to species [quoad speciem], and it is not required that it have existence in act; but from this, that the first disposition [dispositio] itself of the causes has been made, the species of the object is thence determined; namely [puta], which of the two parts of the object is to be future, even if [& si] existence has been communicated to neither:

Meministi enim a te ipso illatum nihil aliter contingere posse quam contingat; supposita hac prima causarum dispositione. Quod si hic mundus etiam non potuit non esse, ut praedicat nobis Ereunius, vides ab ipso decreto Dei, immo ab ipsa aeterna essentia & contradictione quam habet ad non essendum, originem trahere futuritionem singulorum per tantam tamque diffusam causarum inter se connexarum propaginem.

For you remember [it] was inferred [illatum] by you yourself that nothing can happen otherwise than it happens, this first disposition of the causes being supposed. But if this world too could not not be, as Ereunius proclaims [praedicat] to us, you see that from the very decree of God, nay from the very eternal essence and the contradiction which it has to not-being, the futurition of single [things] draws its origin, through so great and so diffused a propagation [propaginem] of causes connected among themselves.

Asphal. Decepisti me, Andabata, sed ita ut non sim captus, sed potius e contra recreatus: video enim unde veritatem habere possint propositiones de futuro contingenti, quod prius impossibile aestimabam.

Asphal. You have deceived me, Andabata, but so that I am not caught, but rather on the contrary refreshed [recreatus]: for I see whence propositions about the contingent future can have truth, which before I esteemed impossible.

terms: Stoic fate / the fate of the Stoics

Stoic heimarmenê; Asphalius, speaking ‘in the name of’ the Stoics, defines it as ‘the necessity of contradiction’ (p. 346) — i.e. logical fatalism from the principle of bivalence, the argument of Aristotle, De interpretatione 9, and of Diodorus/Chrysippus (Cicero, De fato).
Aristotelian logic: of two contradictories one is necessarily true and the other false; the debate is whether this holds determinately of future contingents (De int. 9).
from the force of the contradiction
The phrase recurs throughout; White makes ‘force’ of contradiction a quasi-causal notion that needs a cause in act.
‘in general / in particular’; also distributive vs determinate.
Scholastic distinction (disjunction true ‘in common’ vs one disjunct true ‘determinately’).
Terms of the scholastic future-contingents debate (determinate truth).

notes: Unit: Dialogue III, Knot x, part 1 of 2. PDF pp. 354–364 = printed pp. 343–353, from Asphalius’ ‘Ego vero reclamo huic iniquae duorum consensioni’ (p. 343, margin ‘Nodus X. Fundamentum fati Stoicorum.’) to Asphalius’ ‘…quod prius impossibile aestimabam.’ (p. 353). Offset +11 holds (p. 353 = PDF 364). Signatures Xx (p. 345), Xx ij (p. 347), Xx iij (p. 349), Yy (p. 353). Part 2 begins with Andabata’s ‘Verum tu me prorsus coepisti’ (p. 353), beside a margin ‘Veritate propositionum de…’ (continued on p. 354); Knot xi is listed in the table at p. 362.

Uncertain readings and constructions: (1) p. 346 ‘si in proportionibus sit contradictio’ — clearly printed ‘proportionibus’; taken as a misprint for ‘propositionibus’, marked {?proportionibus}. (2) p. 346 a speech headed ‘Andab. Tu vero, Andabata, …’ — a misprinted speaker head; the sense and alternation require Asphalius; the Latin is kept as printed with [sic], the English heads it [Asphal.]. (3) p. 343 ‘utrique scribo’ — literally ‘I write to each’; perhaps ‘I address [my argument] to both’; sense uncertain. (4) p. 346 ‘modo gesta verbis non responsent’ — read as ironic ‘only, the deeds do not answer to the words’ (fine words without proof); could also be taken as a wish ‘provided the deeds do not fail to answer’. (5) p. 347 ‘Novi, itaque ignarus iam dudum sum quo tendas’ — read as irony (‘and so, of course, I have long been ignorant where you are heading’, i.e. I have long known). (6) p. 350–351 ‘futuritio ex suppositione est saltem causae ex ipsa natura sua’ — ‘causae’ (genitive, across the line-break cau-|sae) taken as ‘belongs to a cause’; the construction is compressed. (7) p. 351 ‘quae necdum positae erunt’ — the future tense is odd (‘will not yet have been posited’); kept literally. (8) p. 353 ‘& si neutri communicata sit existentia’ — taken as etsi (‘even if’). (9) Punctuation: questions printed with full stops (p. 346 ‘Nonne … testatur.’, p. 349 ‘Non ipse tu modo supponis …’) are translated as questions. No illegible readings.

Verification pass: the Latin was re-read sentence by sentence against the page images (margin p. 352 zoomed at 300 dpi) and against the English. The check produced 5 corrections: (i) p. 347 ‘nunquam non potuerunt fieri non futura’ — first drafted ‘could never become not-future’, dropping one negative; restored to ‘never could they not become not-future’ as printed (double negation kept literal); (ii) p. 348 ‘quorum duorum hoc ultimum … prius vero …’ — first drafted with ‘the former’ and ‘the latter’ swapped; corrected (hoc ultimum = this last excludes the extrinsic cause; prius = the former excludes governing); (iii) p. 349 ‘necessum est’ — first rendered ‘it is needful’; set to ‘it is necessary [necessum est]’ for consistency with necessitas; (iv) p. 352 ‘per alias contingentes’ — first drafted ‘through other contingents’; [causes] supplied, since contingentes agrees with an understood causas; (v) p. 349 ‘Habet utique’ — first drafted ‘It is, certainly’; made literal (‘It is so disposed [habet]’), echoing sese habet in the question.

Conventions: as in previous units (see glossary.md). Long speeches are split at sense-breaks (continuation rows carry no speaker head). conditor = founder; gubernator = governor; futuritio = futurition; ex suppositione = from supposition; signate = designatedly; se habere = be disposed / stand; ratio (concept) = notion, (argument) = reason, (account) = account.
